summary.text: Gives the executive summary, explaining that few countries have adopted the 2016 WHO innovations of birth testing, point-of-care NAT and enhanced postnatal prophylaxis, and that this update draws on 2017 and 2018 expert meetings to describe changing strategies for infant HIV. It is followed by a list of abbreviations.

sections.extract: 1.1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY New HIV infections in children continue to occur globally and timely diagnosis and treatment of infants and children living with HIV remain critically important. The 2016 WHO ARV Consolidated Guidelines presented some innovative approaches, such as the use of nucleic acid testing (NAT) at or around birth for earlier diagnosis of HIV in infants, the introduction of point-of-care (POC) NAT for

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: Describes the status of paediatric HIV, noting the drop in new child infections under the Global Plan but 180 000 new infections in 2017, and the shift of mother-to-child transmission towards the postnatal period. A figure shows early and later transmission rates in the priority countries of the Start Free, Stay Free, AIDS Free framework.

sections.extract: 2.1 BACKGROUND 2.1.1 Current status quo regarding pediatric HIV The Global Plan Towards the Elimination of New HIV Infections among Children by 2015 and Keeping their Mothers Alive initiative has had a substantial impact, leading to a 60% reduction in new pediatric HIV infections in 21 high-burden countries in sub-Saharan Africa.1,2 Nevertheless, the burden of new HIV infections in children remains significant: in

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Notes that only about half of children living with HIV were on treatment in 2017 and that untreated infants face very high mortality, then sets out the reasons for this technical update. It explains that falling transmission rates and low viremia have reduced the predictive value of nucleic acid tests, so false-positive infant diagnoses are increasingly reported. The page raises the question of introducing an indeterminate result range for early infant diagnosis.

sections.extract: Furthermore, although pediatric ART coverage has notably improved since 2010, only 51% of the estimated 1.8 million children living with HIV were receiving ART by the end of 2017.3 HIV-infected infants and younger children have an exceptionally high mortality without treatment, approximately 30% by the first year and 50% by their second year of life.9 Many HIV-related deaths in infants can be avoided by early

sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Reports a systematic review indicating that a sizeable share of non-negative infant test results are indeterminate, most of which prove negative on retesting, and explains the use of PCR cycle thresholds to define an indeterminate range. It closes with definitions of terms such as indeterminate, non-negative and discordant results.

sections.extract: A systematic review of 32 studies using an indeterminate range found 14 753 non-negative test results of which 2 436 (16.5% [95% CI 15.9–17.1%]) were indeterminate (data unpublished); one study14 that reported the final diagnoses of indeterminate cases found that 76% of infants with an initial indeterminate test result were negative on repeat testing, suggesting these infants were not HIV-infected despite the

summary.text: Discusses confirmatory testing, noting that prequalified point-of-care infant diagnosis devices perform comparably to laboratory tests and can be used to confirm positive results, and covers management of discordant results and treatment interruption. A summary box stresses immediate retesting of indeterminate results, team support for repeated cases and confirmatory testing of all positives.

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Covers the rollout of point-of-care early infant diagnosis, citing studies in Malawi and Mozambique showing faster results and earlier treatment, and lists lessons on device placement and site selection. It also addresses birth testing, and a box urges national regulators to approve the two prequalified technologies quickly.

sections.extract: 3.1.3 Implementation of POC EID testing The 2016 WHO ARV Consolidated Guidelines10 recommend the use of NAT technologies for early infant HIV testing that have been developed and validated for use at or near the point-of-care. POC EID provides the opportunity to reduce test turnaround times, limit patient loss along the HIV testing cascade, reduce infant mortality and facilitate task shifting to lower cadres of

sections.title: Page 9

summary.text: Summarizes challenges of HIV testing at birth, such as staffing, sampling newborns and linkage to treatment, and describes country experiences in South Africa and Kenya. It stresses linking infected newborns to treatment with suitable formulations and the need for good leadership and coordination.

sections.extract: • Birth testing is acceptable to mothers, but challenges arise from the increased human resources needed, the difficulty of collecting blood samples in newborns, the need to ensure sample collection outside of standard working hours and deliver results, linkage to ART and the nature of the EID system as a whole (stock-outs, referral mechanisms, delayed results). sections.title: Page 11

summary.text: Addresses interpretation of the 9-month infant test and simplification of the testing algorithm, explaining how maternal treatment, infant prophylaxis and late maternal infection can make rapid antibody tests unreliable for exposure or infection status. It sets out key points: testing mothers to establish exposure, not treating a negative infant result after 4 months as definitive, and confirming positive results with NAT.

sections.extract: 3.1.5 Ensuring accurate interpretation of the 9-month test and simplifying the testing algorithm The 2016 WHO ARV Consolidated Guidelines recommend that RDTs should be used to assess HIV exposure among infants younger than 4 months, while HIV exposure among infants 4–18 months old should be ascertained by testing the mother. When testing of the mother is not possible, current guidelines emphasize the importance of

sections.title: Page 12

summary.text: Explains the WHO recommendation of dual AZT and nevirapine prophylaxis for high-risk infants, extended to 12 weeks in breastfeeding infants, and defines which infants are high risk. It discusses the rationale based on mothers reaching viral suppression and gives guidance on whether to continue infant prophylaxis when maternal adherence is poor. It advises that prophylaxis, once stopped, should not be restarted and that attention should go to the causes of poor maternal adherence.

sections.extract: 3.2. ARV use for prevention and treatment of HIV in infants 3.2.1 Implementation challenges to providing ePNP for high-risk infants The 2016 WHO ARV Consolidated Guidelines recommend a dual regimen of AZT and NVP which can be extended for up to 12 weeks in breastfeeding infants deemed to be at high risk of MTCT. A high-risk infant is defined as an infant whose mother was first identified as HIV-infected at delivery

sections.title: Page 13

summary.text: Considers giving high-risk infants presumptive triple-drug treatment as enhanced prophylaxis, paired with testing before it starts, and describes the limited and complex options for early infant treatment. It weighs the use of fixed-dose combination tablets, noting issues such as unwanted lamivudine exposure and the need to split tablets into quarters.

sections.extract: As more effective treatments increasingly come to be used in pregnant women, we can expect decreasing MTCT rates. However, some women will still be diagnosed late or have incident infections and this group is likely to drive most new cases of HIV transmission to infants, owing to the high level of maternal virus in the absence of treatment. One possibility would be to provide “presumptive treatment” as postnatal

sections.title: Page 14

summary.text: Discusses integrating care for HIV-exposed infants into maternal and child health services and linked information systems, while noting pressure on staff. It also describes the role of community services and networks of women living with HIV, and lists patient-level and health system interventions to keep infants in the testing cascade.

sections.extract: provide opportunities to strengthen service delivery for HIV-exposed infants. Integration within a well established maternal, neonatal, and child services platform, which traditionally provides services closest to clients, facilitates mother-infant pair follow-up and reduces the cost and time-visit burden on clients. The integrated information systems that link mother and infant information improve client tracking

sections.title: Page 15

summary.text: Lists key research questions on infant diagnosis, prophylaxis and treatment, such as the value of birth testing and an indeterminate range and the dosing of new ARVs for newborns. A closing section calls for strengthening existing systems, tailoring strategies to context and gathering more programme evidence.

sections.extract: Annex 4: Algorithm for risk assessment This algorithm was developed to support risk assessment at the time of delivery and to help identify infants at high and low risk: Infants at low risk should be given standard prophylaxis (NVP or AZT alone for 4–6 weeks) while those at high risk should be given ePNP. narratives.en: Stacked horizontal bar chart of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rates in 2017 in the 22 Start Free, Stay Free, AIDS Free priority countries, split into 6-week transmission rate (dark blue) and post-6-week transmission rate (light blue), with totals at the bar ends; the render is cropped at the left and also includes body text above. Totals range from 26% in Indonesia, Angola and Nigeria to 5% in South Africa and Botswana; for example Indonesia 19% + 7%, Nigeria 14% + 14%, and Botswana 3% + 2%.
narratives.ar: مخطط شريطي أفقي مكدّس لمعدلات انتقال العدوى من الأم إلى الطفل في عام 2017 في البلدان الاثنين والعشرين ذات الأولوية ضمن إطار «البداية الحرة، والبقاء أحراراً، والتحرّر من الإيدز»، مقسّمة إلى معدل الانتقال حتى 6 أسابيع (أزرق داكن) ومعدل الانتقال بعد 6 أسابيع (أزرق فاتح)، مع المجاميع في نهاية الأشرطة؛ والصورة مقتطعة من اليسار وتتضمن أيضاً نصاً في الأعلى. تتراوح المجاميع بين 26% في إندونيسيا وأنغولا ونيجيريا و5% في جنوب أفريقيا وبوتسوانا؛ مثلاً إندونيسيا 19% + 7%، ونيجيريا 14% + 14%، وبوتسوانا 3% + 2%.
narratives.zh: 堆积水平条形图，显示2017年“无艾起点、无艾成长、无艾生活”框架下22个重点国家的母婴传播率，分为6周传播率（深蓝色）和6周后传播率（浅蓝色），条形末端标有合计；渲染图左侧被裁切，上方还包含正文文字。合计从印度尼西亚、安哥拉和尼日利亚的26%到南非和博茨瓦纳的5%不等；例如印度尼西亚19%+7%，尼日利亚14%+14%，博茨瓦纳3%+2%。
narratives.es: Gráfico de barras horizontales apiladas de las tasas de transmisión maternoinfantil (TMI) en 2017 en los 22 países prioritarios del marco Start Free, Stay Free, AIDS Free, dividido en tasa de transmisión a las 6 semanas (azul oscuro) y tasa de transmisión posterior a las 6 semanas (azul claro), con los totales al final de las barras; la imagen está recortada a la izquierda e incluye también texto en la parte superior. Los totales van del 26% en Indonesia, Angola y Nigeria al 5% en Sudáfrica y Botswana; por ejemplo, Indonesia 19% + 7%, Nigeria 14% + 14% y Botswana 3% + 2%.
narratives.fr: Diagramme à barres horizontales empilées des taux de transmission mère-enfant (TME) en 2017 dans les 22 pays prioritaires du cadre Start Free, Stay Free, AIDS Free, répartis entre taux de transmission à 6 semaines (bleu foncé) et taux de transmission après 6 semaines (bleu clair), avec les totaux en bout de barre ; le rendu est rogné à gauche et inclut aussi du texte au-dessus.
